Second Opium War: 1856–1860 war between British–French forces and China.
In 1968 she became the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, and in 1972 the first Black major-party presidential candidate — who was she?
Formed after the October Revolution of 1917 and dissolved in 1991, this Moscow-based superpower was the largest country on Earth by area — which one?
Soviet Union: Country in Eurasia from 1922 to 1991.
A 19th-century Muslim reformer and educationist in British India, he's widely credited as the father of the two-nation theory that underpinned the Pakistan movement — which figure was he?
Syed Ahmad Khan: Indian reformer and social activist (1817–1898)
Often appearing as a crow and said to wash the bloodstained clothes of those fated to die in battle, which Irish goddess of war and fate is known as the 'phantom queen'?
The Morrígan: Figure from Irish mythology.
This British Labour politician sat in the Commons for 47 of 51 years and later presided over the Stop the War Coalition — though for a stretch he was known as The Viscount Stansgate — who is he?
Tony Benn: British politician and activist (1925–2014)
This Germanic people allied with Rome during the Marcomannic Wars before later conquering and ruling Roman North Africa until 534 CE — who were they?
Serving under Jimmy Carter, this Minnesota senator became the 42nd U.S. vice president and the Democratic Party's presidential nominee in 1984 — who is he?
Walter Mondale: Vice President of the United States from 1977 to 1981.

Dubbed 'the Great Commoner' and 'the Boy Orator' for his faith in ordinary people and his thundering rhetoric, this Nebraskan was the Democrats' presidential nominee three times — in 1896, 1900, and 1908. Who was he?
This retired Turkish general served as the 30th Chief of the General Staff of the Turkish Armed Forces before becoming Minister of National Defense — who is he?
Yaşar Güler: Turkish general and politician (born 1954)
Son of Edward the Elder, this ruler is regarded by modern historians as the first King of England; he never married and was succeeded by his half-brother Edmund — who is he?
Æthelstan: King of the English from 927 to 939.

Calouste Gulbenkian (born 1869) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four. Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Which of these four is the oldest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is a physicist?
Max von Laue is a physicist.
Which of these is a chemist?
Alfred Nobel is a chemist. Alfred Bernhard Nobel ( noh-BEL; Swedish: [ˈǎlːfrɛd nʊˈbɛlː]; 21 October 1833 – 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
What is the atomic number of Einsteinium?
Einsteinium: Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Es and atomic number 99 and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element.
In what year was Hamish Harding born?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year was Vikram Sarabhai born?
Vikram Sarabhai: Often regarded as the "Father of Indian space program", Sarabhai was honored with Padma Bhushan in 1966 and the Padma Vibhushan (posthumously) in 1972.
In what year was Johann Wolfgang von Goethe born?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (28 August 1749 – 22 March 1832) was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
In what year did Aryabhata die?
Aryabhata: The claim that Nalanda used to be located in Kusamapura/Pataliputra also cannot be proven.
In what year did Ivan Pavlov die?
Ivan Pavlov: Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
In what year was Iodine discovered?
Iodine: Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
In what year was Nickel discovered?
Nickel: Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.

In which country is Fish and chips?
Fish and chips: United Kingdom. Fish and chips is a hot dish consisting of battered and fried fish, served with chips.
Who is credited with discovering Norma?

Norma (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for normal, referring to a right angle, and is variously considered to represent a rule, a carpenter's square, a set square or a level.
Who is credited with discovering Aspartame?
Aspartame: James M. Schlatter. Aspartame is an artificial, non-saccharide sweetener commonly used as a sugar substitute in foods and beverages.
Who is credited with discovering Histamine?
Histamine: Henry Hallett Dale. Histamine or histamin is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.
About 5 million tonnes of acetic acid are produced annually largely to make this compound, most commonly in polymer form — what is it?
Acetate is a salt formed by the combination of acetic acid with a base (e.g. sodium hydroxide), an ester of acetic acid, or the anion CH3COO- found in solution.
First approved in the United States in 1966, this xanthine oxidase inhibitor treats high uric acid levels linked to gout, kidney stones, and chemotherapy — what medication is it?
Allopurinol is a medication used to decrease high blood uric acid levels.
Nicknamed the 'nail mosquito,' this genus — first classified in 1818 — is the sole mosquito genus known to carry human malaria — which genus is it?
Anopheles is a genus of mosquito first described by the German entomologist J. W. Meigen in 1818.

Caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, this infection hides in plain sight — over 85% of cases have no symptoms at all — yet in children it can stunt weight gain and trigger learning problems. What's the disease called?
Ascariasis is a disease caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. The eggs hatch in the intestines, the larvae burrow through the gut wall, and migrate to the lungs via the blood.
Facing a shortage of staff, this American lawyer volunteered himself as chief prosecutor at the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg and later championed an International Criminal Court — who was he?
Ben Ferencz (March 11, 1920 - April 7, 2023) was an American lawyer.
This leafy vegetable forms no head, just green blades atop pale bulbous stalks, with a flavor often compared to a mix of spinach and water chestnut — what vegetable is it?

Bok choy (American English, Canadian English, and Australian English), pak choi (British English, South African English, and Caribbean English) or pok choi is a type of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp.
Unlike ordinary weight loss from undereating, this illness-linked syndrome strips away muscle mass in ways good nutrition can't fully undo — what condition is it?
Cachexia is a syndrome that occurs in people with certain illnesses, causing muscle loss that cannot be fully reversed with improved nutrition.
This clouding of the eye's lens is responsible for nearly 40 percent of blindness cases worldwide, often causing halos around lights and trouble seeing at night — what condition is it?
Cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye that impairs vision.
Linked to repeated head trauma, this worsening neurodegenerative disease turns up in boxers and footballers — and even in soccer players, largely from heading the ball. What is it?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated trauma to the head. The encephalopathy symptoms can include behavioral problems, mood problems, and problems with thinking.
This group of mostly evergreen, cone-bearing trees and shrubs reproduces via wind-pollination, with the seeds themselves also scattered by the wind — what plant group is it?
Conifer are a group of vascular plants and a subset of gymnosperms.
Native to Mexico and Central America and related to the sunflower and daisy, this genus of 49 tuberous perennial species blooms in nearly every color except blue — which genus?
Dahlia is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants native to Mexico and Central America.
Tamed in Africa millennia ago and still hauling loads across the developing world, which equine traces its lineage to Equus africanus?
Donkey is a domesticated equine. It was domesticated in Africa some 5000–7000 years ago, and has been used mainly as a working animal since that time.
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of her country's central bank, and was ranked among Forbes' most powerful women in 2019 — who is she?
Elvira Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
Botanists use this word for any plant whose leaves stay green and functional through every season, never going bare like a deciduous tree — what is it?
Evergreen is a plant which has foliage that remains green and functional throughout the year.
Holding doctorates in both medicine and philosophy from Pisa by age 21, this Italian naturalist became the "founder of experimental biology" by disproving spontaneous generation — who was he?
Francesco Redi (18 February 1626 - 1 March 1697) was an Italian physician, naturalist, biologist, and poet.
The tallest living land animal and the largest ruminant on Earth, this African mammal's closest living relative is the shorter-necked okapi — name the animal?
Giraffe (genus Giraffa) are large African hoofed mammals.

Rooted in a Hebrew word meaning 'to walk' or 'to go,' this collective body of Jewish religious law guides both worship and everyday life, tracing back to biblical commandments and later rabbinic codes — what is it?
Halakha (hah-), is the collective body of Jewish religious laws that are derived from the Written and Oral Torah.

Known taxonomically as Lonicera, this genus of 158 species of arching shrubs and twining vines is native to northern latitudes worldwide, though one of its Asian members has become a notorious invasive pest — what's the plant?
Honeysuckle are arching shrubs or twining vines in the genus Lonicera of the family Caprifoliaceae.

A leading figure among Israel's 'New Historians,' this scholar characterizes the 1948 Palestinian expulsion as a deliberate campaign in his research and now teaches at the University of Exeter — who is he?
Ilan Pappé (born 7 November 1954) is an Israeli historian and political scientist, known for his work on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and as a leading figure among the New Historians.
Trained in biochemistry and physiology before ranging into geography and anthropology, this American author won the 1998 Pulitzer for Guns, Germs, and Steel — who is he?
Jared Diamond (born September 10, 1937) is an American scientist, historian, and author.
Born in 1972, this Canadian atmospheric scientist holds an endowed public-policy chair at Texas Tech and in 2021 became Chief Scientist at the Nature Conservancy — who is she?
Katharine Hayhoe (born 1972) is a Canadian atmospheric scientist.

Which citrus-scented perennial herb in the mint family, whose genus name Melissa comes from the Greek for 'honey bee,' is naturalized worldwide after originating in the Mediterranean and Central Asia?
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
Dubbed the 'Queen of QVC' for her long-running shopping show and holding over 120 patents, this American entrepreneur is also an investor on the reality series Shark Tank — who is she?
Lori Greiner is an American television personality and entrepreneur.

A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered a new element in 1939 by purifying lanthanum laced with actinium, and went on to become the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?
Marguerite Perey (19 October 1909 - 13 May 1975) was a French physicist and a student of Marie Curie.
This British-Lebanese geometer co-founded topological K-theory and lent his name to a famous index theorem — and won both the Fields Medal and the Abel Prize. Who was he?
Michael Atiyah (22 April 1929 - 11 January 2019) was a British-Lebanese mathematician specialising in geometry.
This small green legume, cultivated widely across East and South Asia, is used in both savory dishes and sweet desserts — what is it?
Mung bean (Vigna radiata) is a plant species in the legume family.
Born in the Austro-Hungarian Empire and emigrating to the US in 1884, he's known for pioneering the AC electricity system. Who?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 - 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
This specialized subunit within a biological cell performs a specific function, and may be enclosed in its own membrane or exist without one. What is it?
Organelle is a specialized subunit, within a biological cell, that has a specific function.
Born in the Soviet Union, this entrepreneur co-founded a Russian social network before creating a messaging app with his brother and later relocating to Dubai — who is he?
Pavel Durov (born 10 October 1984) is a technology entrepreneur.

Derived from phosphoric acid by removing one to three protons, this anion or salt takes forms like dihydrogen and hydrogen variants and gives its name to fertilizers and various esters — name the ion?
Phosphate is an anion, salt, functional group or ester derived from a phosphoric acid.
This spiny rodent actually comes in two unrelated varieties, an Old World family and a New World family, whose lookalike coats of keratin quills evolved independently — what animal is it?
Porcupine are large rodents with coats of sharp spines, or quills, that protect them against predators.
This opening at the center of the iris lets light reach the retina and appears black — round in people, a slit in cats, and even a ring shape in some catfish — what's it called?
Pupil is a hole located in the center of the iris of the eye that allows light to strike the retina.
Also called king's crown or Arctic root, this Arctic-growing perennial is widely sold as a supplement even though regulators say its health claims lack solid evidence — which plant?
Rhodiola rosea (commonly golden root, rose root, roseroot, Aaron's rod, Arctic root, king's crown, lignum rhodium, orpin rose) is a perennial flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae.
Once placed in its own plant family before molecular studies folded it into Dracaena, this African and Asian succulent genus includes the plant nicknamed 'devil's tongue' — which genus?

Sansevieria is a historically recognized genus of flowering plants, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia, now included in the genus Dracaena on the basis of molecular phylogenetic studies.
Believed to be bred from the Pekingese and the Lhasa Apso, this toy dog breed originated in Tibet — name the breed?
Shih Tzu is a toy dog or pet dog breed originating from Tibet and believed to be bred from the Pekingese and the Lhasa Apso.
Usually diagnosed in infancy, this rare genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the SMN1 gene is the leading inherited cause of death in babies if left untreated — what condition is it?
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a rare neuromuscular disorder that results in the loss of motor neurons and progressive muscle wasting.
Named for its long, flat, sword-like bill, this large migratory predatory fish loses all its teeth and scales by adulthood and is a popular target among billfish anglers — what is it?
Swordfish (Xiphias gladius), also known as the broadbill in some countries, are large, highly migratory predatory fish characterized by a long, flat, sword-like, pointed bill.
What common name covers a group of spike-leaved flowering plants — mostly in the daisy family — whose prickles evolved purely to ward off hungry herbivores?
Thistle is the common name of a group of flowering plants characterised by leaves with sharp spikes on the margins, mostly in the family Asteraceae.
Several highly prized truffle species belong to this fungal genus, whose lineage is estimated to date to the close of the Jurassic period — which genus?
Tuber (fungus) is a genus in the fungal family Tuberaceae, with estimated molecular dating to the end of the Jurassic period (156 Mya).

This English fashion designer, largely responsible for bringing punk fashion into the mainstream, ran a boutique on King's Road with her partner, whose band helped define the 1970s UK punk scene — who is she?

Vivienne Westwood (ne Swire; 8 April 1941 - 29 December 2022) was an English fashion designer and businesswoman, largely responsible for bringing modern punk and new wave fashions into the mainstream.
This Russian political activist and economist, described as the 'first lady' of her country's opposition, vowed to continue her late husband's work after fleeing into exile. Who is she?
Yulia Navalnaya (ne Abrosimova; born 24 July 1976) is a Russian political activist and economist.

A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, this philosopher wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments before the 1776 work often called the inception of modern economics — who is the "father of economics"?
Adam Smith: Scottish economist and philosopher (1723–1790)
Belonging to the birch family and found throughout the north temperate zone, this genus of about 35 tree and shrub species even reaches into the Andes — what genus is it?
Alder: Genus of flowering plants in the birch family Betulaceae.
Sold under the brand name Norvasc, this long-acting calcium channel blocker treats high blood pressure and variant angina by relaxing and widening the arteries — what's the drug?
Amlodipine: Medication against high blood pressure.
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois won the 2003 Nobel Prize for pioneering work on superfluidity and the quantum physics of low-temperature helium — who was he?
Ranging from a racing tachycardia to a sluggish bradycardia, this catch-all term covers any heartbeat that strays from normal sinus rhythm — what is it called?
Arrhythmia: Group of medical conditions characterized by irregular heartbeat.
This Mexican mole salamander never grows up — it reaches sexual maturity while staying fully aquatic with feathery external gills, skipping metamorphosis entirely. What is it?
Axolotl: Species of salamander. The axolotl (from Classical Nahuatl: āxōlōtl [aːˈʃoːloːtɬ]; Ambystoma mexicanum) is a species of mole salamander.
A largely self-taught naturalist and astronomer born to a free mother in Maryland, he helped survey the District of Columbia and corresponded with Thomas Jefferson — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker: American scientist, surveyor and farmer (1731–1806)

In this distributed ledger, each record holds a cryptographic hash of the one before it, so altering a single block would require rewriting every block that follows — making the data nearly tamper-proof. What is it?
Blockchain: Distributed data store for digital transactions.

Originating from feral Eastern Mediterranean populations, this single wild plant species has been cultivated into an astonishing range of vegetables including broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts. What is it?
Brassica oleracea: Species of plant. Brassica oleracea, also known as wild cabbage in its uncultivated form, is a plant of the family Brassicaceae.
The world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance works by mimicking adenosine's shape and blocking its receptors, keeping you awake — what is this stimulant?

This German-Swedish pharmacist had a knack for discovery — molybdenum, tungsten, barium, chlorine, and arguably oxygen all trace to his bench — but the same hands-on chemistry may have killed him via mercury poisoning. Which unlucky genius is it?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele: Swedish German chemist who discovered oxygen (1742–1786)
Descended from land mammals but now fully aquatic, this group swims via up-and-down tail strokes and includes toothed members capable of echolocation — what group includes whales and dolphins?
With about 3,400 species in over 520 genera, this insect family includes nearly every member of its group except two species in a small sister taxon — which family?
Native to tropical Africa and Asia, this plant genus produces caffeine-rich seeds that are roasted and brewed into one of the world's most valuable traded commodities — which genus?
This group of RNA viruses, named for the club-shaped spikes that crown their surface, causes illnesses ranging from the common cold to SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what are they called?
Coronavirus: Subfamily of viruses in the family Coronaviridae.
Named after the bladder because it was first found in urine, this amino acid carries a thiol group that lets it forge the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together. Which amino acid is it?
Cysteine: Proteinogenic amino acid. Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HS−CH2−CH(NH2)−COOH.
Native to South and Southeast Asia, this is the sole species in its genus and lives in large, non-hierarchical clans with several breeding females — what's this wild canid called?
Dhole: Species of mammal. The dhole ( dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia.

With nearly 24,000 ommatidia in each compound eye and wings usually held flat rather than folded, this iridescent flying insect is often confused with its lighter-bodied damselfly cousins — what is it?
Appointed to the Supreme Court by Barack Obama in 2010, this former Harvard Law dean became the fourth woman ever to serve as a justice — who is she?
Elena Kagan: US Supreme Court justice since 2010.
A rod-shaped gut bacterium that's mostly harmless or even helpful — some strains produce vitamin K2 and fend off nastier microbes — what is its name?
Sold in Italian restaurants as branzino, this slow-growing ocean fish is the most important species farmed commercially in the Mediterranean — what fish is it?
European seabass: Species of fish. It is one of only six species in its family, Moronidae, collectively called the temperate basses.
Belonging to the genus Abies, these evergreen conifers have cones that stand upright like candles and disintegrate at maturity, and some varieties serve as Christmas trees — which conifer genus?
Fir: Genus of coniferous trees. The genus is most closely related to Keteleeria, a small genus confined to eastern Asia.
The largest region of the brain's cerebral hemispheres, this most-forward area contains the primary motor cortex and is separated from the parietal and temporal regions by two grooves — what is it?
Frontal lobe: Part of the brain. The most anterior ventral, orbital end of the frontal lobe is known as the frontal pole, which is one of the three so-called poles of the cerebrum.
Also known as cranesbills for their pointed seed pods, this 422-species genus bears five-petaled, often veined flowers and includes at least one protocarnivorous species — what's the genus?
A U.S. Navy rear admiral who helped develop COBOL, this computer science pioneer wrote what's considered the first computer manual and worked on the Harvard Mark I — who is she?
Grace Hopper: U.S. naval officer and computer scientist (1906–1992)

Coined by psychologist Edward Thorndike, this cognitive bias describes how a positive impression in one area, like someone's looks, skews our judgment of them in unrelated areas — what is this bias called?
Halo effect: Tendency for positive impressions to contaminate other evaluations.
With over 800 species lugging borrowed snail shells to shield their soft, non-calcified abdomens, this crustacean is essentially homeless without a hand-me-down home. What is it?
Stretching about a meter from crown to tail-tip, this deep-blue South American parrot is the largest of its kind and can be mistaken for a smaller relative — which vulnerable parrot?
Co-creator of the AlexNet neural network and former chief scientist at OpenAI, this computer scientist has won NeurIPS's Test of Time Award three years running — who is he?

This Mexican neurophysiologist studied shamanism, meditation, and telepathy through the scientific method, wrote more than 50 books on the subjects, and then vanished without a trace in December 1994 — who was he?
Jacobo Grinberg: Mexican pseudoscientist, neurophysiologist and psychologist.
This English mathematician dreamed up the cellular automaton known as the Game of Life and spent his later years at Princeton — who was he?
Also called Bushman's tea, the leaves of this East African shrub are chewed as a recreational stimulant, most popular among Somalis and Yemenis — what is it?
This probability principle explains why a casino might lose money on a single spin of roulette but reliably earns a predictable percentage over many thousands of spins. What is it called?
Law of large numbers: Averages of repeated trials converge to the expected value.
Instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission, this Austrian-Swedish physicist fled Nazi Germany in 1938 after losing her post under the Nuremberg Laws — who is she?

Fired by IBM in 1968 for revealing her intent to transition — an apology that took until 2020 — this computer scientist had already invented dynamic instruction handling behind modern out-of-order execution. Who was she?
Lynn Conway: American computer scientist and electrical engineer (1938–2024)

Originally hoping to become an engineer, this Italian physician became one of the first women to graduate from medical school in Italy and later devised an influential educational philosophy — who is she?
Maria Montessori: Italian physician and educator (1870–1952)

Encompassing conditions marked by a clinically significant disturbance in thinking, emotional regulation, or behavior that causes real distress or impaired functioning, this broad psychiatric category has causes that remain often unclear — what is the umbrella term for it?
Nicknamed 'Foxbat' by NATO and built largely from stainless steel, this Soviet interceptor still holds the altitude record for an airbreathing piloted aircraft at 38 km — which jet?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Family of interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft.
Born in China and educated at MIT and Stanford, this billionaire engineer founded Taiwan's dominant chipmaker, serving as its CEO from 1987 to 2005 — who is he?
Morris Chang: Taiwanese businessman and electrical engineer (born 1931)
This chronic neurological disorder scrambles the sleep-wake cycle, bringing on excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, and sudden episodes of muscle collapse called cataplexy — what is it?
Narcolepsy: Human sleep disorder. Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that impairs the ability to regulate sleep–wake cycles, and specifically impacts REM (rapid eye movement) sleep.
Unlike its more predictably spreading cousin, this group of blood cancers can appear in multiple parts of the body at once and cause enlarged lymph nodes, fevers, and night sweats — which condition?
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of cancer of lymph nodes.
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors are shaped by their consequences — strengthened by reinforcement, weakened by punishment or extinction. What is it called?
Operant conditioning: Type of associative learning process for behavioral modification.
This B vitamin's name comes from the Greek for "from everywhere," since it turns up in nearly all foods, and animals need it to build coenzyme A — what is it?
Developed at Abbott Laboratories in 1930 and nicknamed 'yellow jackets' for its brand-name capsule color, this barbiturate is used in veterinary euthanasia and some U.S. executions — what drug is it?
Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria run this light-powered process, splitting water to release oxygen as a byproduct while banking energy in sugars like glucose. What is it called?
Photosynthesis: Biological process to convert light into chemical energy.
Whether natural silk or synthetic nylon, this class of polymer is defined by repeating units joined through amide bonds — what is it?
Polyamide: Macromolecule with repeating units linked by amide bonds.
Genetic studies trace this most widely cultivated apricot species to Central Asia, though its scientific name nods to a country in the Caucasus — what is it?
Prunus armeniaca: Species of apricot. The native range is somewhat uncertain due to its extensive prehistoric cultivation.
About the size of a house cat, this nocturnal herbivorous marsupial thrives on Rottnest Island near Perth and is the only member of its genus — what is it?
Quokka: Small marsupial from southwestern Australia.
Typically striking two to four weeks after a strep throat, this inflammatory disease can attack the heart, joints, skin and brain — and may permanently scar the heart valves. What is it?
Native to India, Nepal and Sri Lanka, this tiny feline is one of the smallest members of its family, and has been listed as Near Threatened since 2016 due to deforestation — which species?
Rusty-spotted cat: Small wild cat species native to South Asia.
This genus contains most of the world's familiar bushy-tailed tree squirrels, found across North America, Europe, temperate Asia, and Central and South America — which genus?
Native to East Asia, this cultivated mushroom is also known as the black mushroom or Chinese mushroom — name the fungus?

Native to Eurasia and found in Paleolithic-era deposits in ancient Britain, this flowering plant's ripe berries and cooked leaves are eaten in some regions despite its nightshade family's fearsome reputation — what is it?
Solanum nigrum: Species of flowering plant in the nightshade family. The plant was known and mentioned by ancient herbalists, including Dioscorides.
This Taiwanese-American engineer co-founded YouTube and served as its CTO before later building the video app MixBit — who is he?
Native to the Balkan Peninsula, this fragrant flowering shrub in the olive family is cultivated widely across Europe and North America for its clusters of purple or white blooms — which species?
Syringa vulgaris: Plant species in the olive family.
This vertebrate group includes every amphibian and amniote — even limbless descendants like snakes, which still count as members through their four-limbed ancestry — what's the clade called?
Tetrapod: Clade of the first four-limbed vertebrates and their descendants.
Known for dry, bumpy skin studded with parotoid glands and a more terrestrial lifestyle than its smooth-skinned cousins, what is this amphibian called?
Toad: Common name for certain frogs, especially of the family Bufonidae.
NATO code-named 'Careless,' this three-engined Soviet airliner once carried half of Aeroflot's passengers and could operate from unpaved gravel airstrips in Arctic conditions — which aircraft?
Tupolev Tu-154: Soviet and Russian medium-range trijet airliner.
Unlike arteries, most of these thin-walled blood vessels carry deoxygenated blood back toward the heart — what are they?
Vein: Blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart.
With a distinctive pale eye and grey nape against black plumage, this small, gregarious member of the crow family was first formally described by Linnaeus — name the bird?
Western jackdaw: Species of bird in the crow family Corvidae.
As Jimmy Carter's National Security Advisor from 1977 to 1981, this Polish-American scholar organized the Trilateral Commission and oversaw normalized ties with Communist China — who was he?
Zbigniew Brzezinski: Polish-American diplomat and political scientist (1928–2017)
